layers.name: CLI Application Layer
layers.description: User-facing tuck command handlers and command-line orchestration that dispatch file, package, source, and root operations.

layers.name: Core Domain and Planning Layer
layers.description: Core tuck domain types, manifest and package resolution, package references, source planning, and status calculations that drive command behavior.

layers.name: State and Persistence Layer
layers.description: State file schemas, path derivation, validation, marshaling, and testhook variants for tuck project state persistence.

layers.name: Shared Utilities Layer
layers.description: Cross-cutting error handling and path helper packages used by the domain, planning, state, and CLI layers.

layers.name: Error Generation Tool Layer
layers.description: The errgen developer command and generator implementation that produce typed application error helper code for internal packages.

layers.name: Test and Acceptance Layer
layers.description: Unit tests, package tests, acceptance harnesses, and txtar script fixtures that verify tuck behavior end to end.

layers.name: Documentation Layer
layers.description: Project guidance, CLI specifications, testing strategy, backlog, and milestone specs that explain intended tuck behavior.

layers.name: Configuration Layer
layers.description: Go module metadata, editor settings, mise and codebook configuration, and Understand Anything project configuration for the repository.

tour.title: CLI Entry Point
tour.description: Start in the CLI application layer, because the project entry point named in the prompt is not present in the merged graph and this file is the closest application entry node. The main application wiring shows how tuck begins execution, establishes the command surface, and hands control to the rest of the CLI package. Use this as the orientation point for the command handlers, output behavior, and domain workflows that follow.

tour.title: CLI Contract
tour.description: After seeing where the application starts, read the CLI specification to understand the behavior the code is trying to provide. This documentation gives the user-facing vocabulary for source, package, file, status, and root operations, so later code stops can be read as implementations of that contract. It is the tour's product-level map in a repository without a README overview.
tour.languageLesson: Markdown specifications are useful architecture artifacts: they define behavior in user terms before the implementation spreads that behavior across command handlers, domain types, and tests.

tour.title: Command Families
tour.description: The command files break the CLI contract into focused handler groups for source registry operations, package operations, and individual file operations. Building on the entry point from Step 1, these files are where parsed commands become calls into state, package resolution, and planning logic. Reading them together shows the main vertical slices of tuck's user workflow.

tour.title: Arguments and Output
tour.description: Before diving into the core domain, understand how the CLI accepts input and reports results. The arguments, flags, exit, and output modules form the boundary between internal decisions and the terminal UX, and output.go is structurally broad according to the fan-out ranking. This step explains how command handlers stay focused while shared code handles presentation and process exits.

tour.title: Domain and Manifest
tour.description: The domain and manifest layer defines the vocabulary the command handlers rely on: roots, package metadata, and the tuck.toml contract. The milestone spec provides the intended manifest behavior, while the code loads and validates that behavior for runtime use. This is the bridge from CLI verbs to the project model tuck operates on.
tour.languageLesson: Go's internal/ directory limits imports from outside the repository tree, which helps keep domain packages as private implementation details of this CLI.

tour.title: State Persistence
tour.description: Tuck also needs machine-local state for configured source trees, paths, validation, and serialization. These files are high fan-in nodes in the graph, meaning many parts of the project depend on the state contract being stable. Read this layer after the manifest layer to distinguish repository configuration from per-machine registry state.

tour.title: Package Resolution
tour.description: Once sources and manifests are known, the packages layer discovers package contents from configured source trees. The graph ranks packages.go as one of the broadest files by fan-out, which makes it a key overview stop for how tuck resolves what can be used, adopted, or inspected. walk.go complements it by representing the filesystem traversal side of package discovery.

tour.title: Planning Changes
tour.description: The plan layer turns resolved packages and file requests into concrete filesystem mutation plans. The use, adopt, eject, and apply files form the core write path: decide what should change, then apply those changes safely. This is where the command families from Step 3 become operational behavior on disk.

tour.title: Status Evaluation
tour.description: Status is the read-oriented counterpart to the mutation planning layer. These files classify target files and package entries so users can understand the current relationship between their project and configured tuck sources. The status milestone spec ties the implementation back to the documented CLI behavior introduced earlier.

tour.title: Shared Utilities
tour.description: The shared utility packages support nearly every layer without owning a product workflow themselves. pathutil centralizes normalization, containment, target translation, and symlink payload helpers, while apperr provides typed application-error wrappers used across packages. Understanding these utilities makes the higher-level code easier to read because repeated path and error patterns become recognizable.

tour.title: Error Generation
tour.description: The repository includes a developer tool for generating typed package error helper code. This explains the generated apperr_gen.go files that appear throughout state, manifest, packages, and plan packages, and keeps shared error handling consistent. The mise configuration belongs here because it records the local workflow tasks for generation, checks, and development automation.
tour.languageLesson: Generated Go code is commonly committed when it is part of the build contract; the generator becomes infrastructure that maintains consistency rather than runtime application logic.

tour.title: Acceptance Testing
tour.description: Finish with the test and acceptance layer to see how the documented CLI contract is verified end to end. The harness and suites execute txtar script fixtures that model real command scenarios for foundation, source, and package behavior. Reading these after the implementation shows how tuck protects its workflows across CLI parsing, state, planning, and filesystem effects.
tour.languageLesson: txtar fixtures bundle files and scripts into one text archive, which makes command-line acceptance tests reproducible and easy to review in code review.

tour.title: Module Configuration
tour.description: Close the tour with the repository configuration that supports day-to-day development. go.mod and go.sum define the Go module and dependency checksums, while the codebook configuration documents local spelling rules used by project tooling. This final stop connects the architecture you have learned to the practical setup files contributors touch when building, testing, and maintaining tuck.
tour.languageLesson: go.mod declares the module path and required dependencies, while go.sum records cryptographic checksums so dependency resolution is reproducible.
